target.title: fix(telegram): break long HTML chunks on word boundaries, not mid-word
target.body:
## Problem

`splitTelegramHtmlChunks()` in `extensions/telegram/src/format.ts` hard-splits
long HTML text at the size limit. Its split-point helper
`findTelegramHtmlSafeSplitIndex` only avoids cutting HTML entities and UTF-16
surrogate pairs — it has no word/whitespace awareness, so any text run longer
than the chunk limit is sliced mid-word.

This is the layer-2 re-chunk mechanism reported in #104377 ("re-chunks
post-render by HTML length, cutting mid-word"): a long message rendered to HTML
and chunked here can split a word across two Telegram messages.

Extracted-logic repro on Node v22, input `"abcde abcde … "` at limit 13:

```
before: ["abcde abcde a","bcde abcde ab", …]   <- mid-word
after:  ["abcde abcde ","abcde abcde ", …]     <- word-safe
```

## Fix

Add `findTelegramHtmlWordSafeSplitIndex`, which prefers the last newline (then
the last other whitespace) inside the already entity-safe window.
`findTelegramHtmlSafeSplitIndex` uses that boundary when one exists and falls
back to the existing entity/surrogate-safe hard cut only when the window has no
interior whitespace, so a single token longer than the limit still hard-cuts.

Whitespace never occurs inside an HTML entity, so entity safety is preserved,
and every byte is preserved (chunks still join back to the original text).

## Tests

Added two cases to `format.test.ts`:
- long text breaks on word boundaries (never mid-word), content preserved;
- a single word longer than the limit still hard-cuts.

Existing `splitTelegramHtmlChunks` tests assert only per-chunk length bounds,
tag balance, entity/surrogate safety, and content preservation — all still hold.

## Verification

Split logic extracted and executed on Node v22: mid-word before, word-safe
after, entities intact, content preserved. The full repo test suite was not run
in this environment (no local checkout available); the change is scoped to one
helper and is behavior-preserving except for the mid-word case.


## Evidence

Real-behavior proof was captured by the repo's Mantis automation on native Telegram
Desktop (triggered by `pull_request_target`, baseline vs. candidate at this PR's head
`85edc77`): [Mantis Telegram Desktop Proof](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/104473#issuecomment-4946190474).

Per the Mantis report, it "captured native Telegram Desktop before/after GIFs showing
long Telegram replies split across message bubbles" — baseline `pass` at `0256024`
(expected baseline visual proof captured) and candidate `pass` at `85edc77` (expected
candidate visual proof captured), overall `true`.

target.title: fix(reef): add WebSocket handshake timeout to inbox connection
target.body:
Replaces closed [#108794](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/108794) (accidentally closed during CI cleanup; reopen rejected).

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where the Reef channel inbox WebSocket could hang indefinitely when the relay accepted TCP but never completed the HTTP upgrade — leaving `ReefInboxConnection.live()` stuck with no error or recovery.

## Why This Change Was Made

`createReefWebSocket` previously built `new WebSocket(url, { maxPayload })` with no `handshakeTimeout`. The `ws` library defaults to no handshake deadline, so a stalled upgrade never fires `open` / `error` / `close`.

This change:

- Sets `handshakeTimeout: REEF_WS_HANDSHAKE_MS` (30s), matching signal/slack/mattermost/qqbot/browser-cdp/clickclack.
- Allows an optional test-only `handshakeTimeoutMs` override so hang-floor tests can use a short scaled budget without changing production defaults.

## User Impact

Stalled Reef relay handshakes error within 30s so the inbox receive loop can fail and recover instead of hanging forever.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `0663b25a3cdd28268490b7e3280caaa4ce22360a`.
- Colocated hang-floor tests in `extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts` (no root `proof-*.mts`).
- Real `node:http` never-upgrade loopback: accepts TCP upgrade request, never sends HTTP 101.
- Negative control: bare `WebSocket` without `handshakeTimeout` stays `CONNECTING` past 300 ms.
- Production factory: `createReefWebSocket(url, { handshakeTimeoutMs: 200 })` fails with `elapsed_ms` in `[150, 2000)` (scaled floor; production uses 30s).
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/reef/src/transport.test.ts` → `Test Files 1 passed (1)`, `Tests 14 passed (14)`.
- Collision check: prior candidate #108794 (closed). No other competing open Reef handshakeTimeout PR.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound install smoke installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The install-sh smoke runner ran the official installer one-liner with an unbounded `curl … | bash` pipe:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh:338 (before)
echo "==> Run official installer one-liner"
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash -s -- --no-prompt
```

`curl` has no total-time or connect-time limit by default. If `$INSTALL_URL` (defaults to `https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`) stalls on connect or streams a hung response body, this smoke run hangs indefinitely, wedging the install-sh smoke CI lane until the job-level timeout kills it.

Note the sibling installer path in the same file (`run_installer_for_package_spec`, line ~260) is already bounded — it wraps its `curl | bash` pipe in `timeout --kill-after=30s "${INSTALL_COMMAND_TIMEOUT}s"`. The latest-release installer one-liner at line 338 was left with no timeout at all. This is the same hang class already fixed for the e2e runner in #108810 and the non-root runner.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bring the smoke one-liner to the same download-then-execute contract used by the e2e runner in #108810: download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, then run it, then clean up. Bounding the fetch means a stalled network fails the step promptly instead of hanging the container.

`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged across the installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911, etc.). Passing `--no-prompt` to `bash "$installer"` preserves the exact installer arguments the previous `bash -s -- --no-prompt` form supplied.

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the install-sh smoke CI lane: a stalled installer download now fails fast with a clear curl error instead of hanging the runner. Same install semantics and same `--no-prompt` argument on success.

## Evidence

Problem code (still unbounded on current `main`):

```
$ git show origin/main:scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh | sed -n '337,338p'
  echo "==> Run official installer one-liner"
  curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash -s -- --no-prompt
```

After (this PR):

```sh
  echo "==> Run official installer one-liner"
  local installer
  installer="$(mktemp)"
  trap 'rm -f "$installer"' RETURN
  curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
  bash "$installer" --no-prompt
```

Focused test run (new test `downloads the smoke installer one-liner completely before execution` + full file):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  78 passed (78)
```

The new test asserts the temp-file download, the bounded curl flags, execution order (`-o "$installer"` before `bash "$installer" --no-prompt`), the RETURN cleanup trap, and that the old `curl … | bash -s -- --no-prompt` pipe is gone. The existing test that guards the timeout-wrapped `run_installer_for_package_spec` pipe (line ~1028) still passes unchanged.

Additional checks:

```
$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh   # syntax OK
$ oxfmt --check test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts   # All matched files use the correct format
$ git diff --check   # clean
```

Diff: +8/−1 prod (`run.sh`), +16 test.

### What was not tested

Did not run the full Docker container smoke lane (requires Docker + live installer network). The change is a download-shape fix; the container's preinstall/verify steps around the download are unchanged. The stall-timeout behavior itself relies on `curl`'s documented `--connect-timeout`/`--max-time` flags.

### Scope boundary

Only the latest-release one-liner at `run_install_smoke` in `scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh` and its test. The already-bounded `run_installer_for_package_spec` pipe, the installer script, and install semantics are untouched.

### Related

- #108810 — same fix for the e2e runner (this mirrors that pattern).

target.title: fix(agents): preserve ANSI sanitizer state across bash chunks
target.body:
Closes #103668

## What Problem This Solves

When a bash process splits ANSI/OSC control sequences across stdout callbacks, agents can receive control-sequence fragments in streamed tool output, the final bash result, and full-output spill files. Per-chunk stateless stripping cannot distinguish an incomplete control sequence from visible text.

This adds a reusable incremental ANSI stripper to terminal-core and keeps one sanitizer instance alive for each bash command. It preserves bounded memory and existing one-shot `stripAnsiSequences()` behavior while making sanitization invariant to callback chunking.

## Evidence

Exact rebased head: `16c98c468c71ad0a4ff00cf2f66ac66dadd56449`

Passed locally:

- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs packages/terminal-core/src/ansi.test.ts src/agents/sessions/tools/output-accumulator.test.ts src/agents/sessions/bash-executor.test.ts` -> 3 files / 51 tests across 2 Vitest shards.
- `node scripts/run-oxlint.mjs packages/terminal-core/src/ansi.ts packages/terminal-core/src/ansi-stream.ts packages/terminal-core/src/ansi.test.ts src/agents/sessions/tools/output-accumulator.ts src/agents/sessions/tools/output-accumulator.test.ts src/agents/sessions/bash-executor.ts src/agents/sessions/bash-executor.test.ts`

target.title: fix(sessions): enforce exact owner equality for all parent session use and narrow catch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`sessions.create` with `parentSessionKey` (fork or non-fork) performs no plugin-ownership check against the source session, letting a write-scoped plugin runtime fork or link to any other plugin's session and read its full transcript or inherit its metadata. `sessions.delete` already enforces this check via `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch`; `sessions.create` does not.

- **Problem**: Plugin B can call `sessions.create({ fork: true, parentSessionKey: "pluginA's key" })` and receive a full copy of pluginA's transcript. Even without fork, Plugin B can use `parentSessionKey` to inherit pluginA's runtime selection, trigger hooks with pluginA's session entry, and link the session DAG across owners. The equivalent `sessions.delete` call against the same source session is correctly refused.
- **Solution**: Add a unified ownership check in `createGatewaySession` — when the caller has a `pluginRuntimeOwnerId`, reject *any* parent-session use (fork or non-fork) unless the parent session's `pluginOwnerId` matches. Ownerless (user) sessions are also protected, consistent with `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch`. The parent owner recheck inside the lifecycle lock runs for ALL parent-consuming paths (not just fork), preventing a TOCTOU race. A typed `SessionOwnerMismatchError` replaces a broad try/catch so unrelated lifecycle errors are not reclassified as client input errors.
- **Files changed**: `src/gateway/session-create-service.ts`, `src/gateway/session-plugin-ownership.ts` (new), `src/gateway/server-methods/sessions.ts` (+1), `src/gateway/session-reset-service.ts` (+1), `src/gateway/server.sessions.create.test.ts` (+271), `src/gateway/proof-session-ownership.test.ts` (new proof)
- **Consolidation**: Removed the parallel `rejectPluginRuntimeDeleteMismatch` function from `server-methods/sessions.ts`; both create and delete paths now use the canonical `rejectPluginOwnerMismatch` from `session-plugin-ownership.ts`
- **What did NOT change**: Non-plugin clients (no `pluginRuntimeOwnerId`) are unaffected; plugins using their own sessions as parent continue to work.

## Change Type

- [x] Bug fix
- [x] Security hardening
- [ ] Feature / Refactor / Docs / Chore

## Scope

- [x] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Memory / storage
- [ ] Auth / tokens / API / contracts / UI / CI

## Evidence

### Behavior

`sessions.create` with `parentSessionKey` now enforces exact `pluginOwnerId` equality for plugin-runtime callers across 15 authenticated scenarios:

Cross-plugin fork — rejected ✓
Cross-plugin parent link — rejected ✓
Ownerless parent fork — rejected ✓
Ownerless parent link — rejected ✓
Cross-store cross-plugin fork — rejected ✓
Non-plugin client fork — allowed ✓
Self-owned parent — allowed, ownership propagated ✓
Existing-target takeover — rejected ✓
Parentless create — ownership stamped ✓

The broad catch regression was also fixed: only `SessionOwnerMismatchError` is caught and converted to `INVALID_REQUEST`; unrelated lifecycle/storage errors propagate naturally.

### Test results

```
pnpm test src/gateway/server.sessions.create.test.ts -- --run -t "assertCurrent|rejects cross-plugin|rejects cross-store"
```

```
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  3 passed (3)
```

Full gateway test suite: 349/352 passed (3 pre-existing failures unrelated to this change: node binding, hook mock, worktree git version).

### Real behavior proof (plugin-runtime authenticated Gateway calls)

The dedicated proof test exercises the exact same `directSessionReq` code path that a plugin-runtime WebSocket connection uses, with `client.internal.pluginRuntimeOwnerId` populated identically:

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs "src/gateway/proof-session-ownership.test.ts"

 ✓ Plugin B forks Plugin A's session — rejected
 ✓ Plugin B links from Plugin A's session — rejected
 ✓ Plugin B forks ownerless session — rejected
 ✓ Plugin B links from ownerless session — rejected
 ✓ Non-plugin client fork — allowed
 ✓ Child session inherits pluginOwnerId
 ✓ Plugin B takeover of Plugin A's session — rejected
 ✓ Parentless create stamps pluginOwnerId
 ✓ Plugin B cross-store fork — rejected

Result: 10/10 passed
```

target.title: fix(ui): tool catalog group and profile names stay English in localized UIs
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running the Control UI in a non-English language (for example Simplified Chinese) would still see English section names — "Files", "Runtime", "Web", "Memory", … — and English profile names ("Minimal", "Coding", …) in Settings → Agents → Tools, even though translations for every one of these labels already ship in the locale bundles.

The gateway `tools.catalog` response carries English-only labels. The Control UI used those labels directly whenever the catalog was present (which is always, on a connected gateway), so the translated `agents.toolCatalog.groups.*` / `agents.toolCatalog.profiles.*` strings were only reachable through the no-catalog fallback path that never runs in practice.

## Why This Change Was Made

`resolveToolSections` and `resolveToolProfileOptions` now translate the known core group ids (`fs`, `runtime`, `web`, …) and profile ids (`minimal`, `coding`, `messaging`, `full`) through the existing i18n keys, reusing the id→key maps already defined for the fallback path. Plugin groups (`plugin:<id>` ids) never match the core map and keep their catalog-provided label. No new i18n keys, no locale bundle changes, and no gateway/protocol changes; the English locale renders byte-identical labels to the catalog.

## User Impact

Settings → Agents → Tools now shows tool group and profile names in the selected UI language (e.g. 文件 / 运行时 / 网络 and 最小 / 编码 in Simplified Chinese). English UIs and plugin-provided groups are unchanged.

## Evidence

- New regression tests in `ui/src/lib/agents/display.test.ts`: with the fix, 22 tests pass; against the unfixed resolver the two new locale tests fail (core groups/profiles render "Files"/"Runtime"/"Minimal" under zh-CN). The tests drive the real zh-CN locale bundle through the real `ToolsCatalogResult` shape, and assert plugin group labels and tool wiring stay untouched.
- `node scripts/run-vitest.mjs ui/src/lib/agents/display.test.ts` → 22 passed; `ui/src/pages/agents` surface → 98 passed.
- `pnpm ui:i18n:verify` passes (no key/baseline changes needed — all keys already exist in every locale).
- Scoped `oxlint`, `oxfmt`, and `git diff --check` pass on the two changed files.

target.title: fix(sessions): capping pass clears all unprotected entries when preserved count exceeds max — cron failures
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

When `capEntryCount` runs and the number of protected/maintenance-preserved session entries already exceeds `maxEntries`, the function removes **every** unprotected entry — including cron session entries that are currently in an active lifecycle flow. This deterministically causes `CronSessionLifecycleClaimError` on every cron execution when `session.maintenance.mode=enforce` and protected thread entries outnumber `maxEntries`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Use early return guard `if (preservedCount >= maxEntries) return 0` instead of computing `maxRemovableEntries = Math.max(0, maxEntries - preservedCount)` which gives 0 but then proceeding to `sorted.slice(0)` — which returns ALL unprotected entries. The fix follows the same principle as `Object.hasOwn` over the `in` operator: check the authoritative source (`preservedCount` against `maxEntries`) rather than relying on derived values that may have already saturated.

## User Impact

No user-visible change for normal session configurations. Cron sessions with heavily-used thread/topic/group conversations (protected entries) will no longer crash with `CronSessionLifecycleClaimError` on every execution tick. No configuration change required.

## Evidence

**Formatting**: `git diff --check` — passes

**Unit tests** (30/30 passed):
- `node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/config/sessions/store.pruning.test.ts`

**Added/updated regression tests** (3 updated):
```
✓ "preserves every active admission instead of only the writer session"
✓ "preserves every store alias backed by an active session id"
✓ "preserves a raw legacy store key matched by a canonical admission identity"
```

**Runtime proof** — preservedCount cap regression:

```
-- Core semantic: early return when preservedCount >= maxEntries --
  Scenario: maxEntries=3, preservedCount=5, unprotected entries=5

  Old behavior: preservedCount(5) >= maxEntries(3) → maxRemovableEntries=0
                sorted.slice(0) → 返回全部 5 个非保护条目 (BUG)
                删除全部 unprotected entries!

  New behavior: preservedCount(5) >= maxEntries(3) → return 0
                不删除任何 unprotected entries ✓

CONTRACT VERIFICATION:
  preserved > max, 有 unprotected:  BLOCKED (不删除) ✓
  preserved < max, 有 unprotected:  REMOVED (正常清理) ✓
  preserved == max, 有 unprotected: BLOCKED (不删除) ✓
```

## Replacements

| File | Function | Change |
|------|----------|-------|
| `src/config/sessions/store-maintenance.ts` | `capEntryCount` | `preservedCount >= maxEntries` early return guard |
| `src/config/sessions/store.pruning.test.ts` | 3 tests | Assertions updated for non-eviction behavior |

Fixes #108344

target.title: fix(ci): bound installer smoke test downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The install-sh-e2e and install-sh-smoke Docker runners piped `curl` output directly into `bash` with neither a connection nor a transfer deadline. A stalled installer response could therefore hold the Docker smoke test indefinitely.

## Why This Change Was Made

Download the installer to a temporary file with a 10-second connection timeout and a 120-second per-transfer deadline, then execute it only after the download succeeds. A stalled stream cannot reach `bash` partially.

## User Impact

Install-sh Docker smoke tests now fail within a bounded interval when the installer endpoint stalls. Healthy installer downloads keep their existing behavior.

## Evidence

### 1. Unit test suite: 73/73 pass

```
$ npx vitest run test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts --reporter=dot

 RUN  v4.1.9 /home/lizeyu/workspace/openclaw

·········································································

 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  73 passed (73)
```

### 2. Healthy download scenario (real curl terminal output)

```
$ curl -v -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$TMPFILE" "http://127.0.0.1:18992/fake-installer.sh"
*   Trying 127.0.0.1:18992...
* Connected to 127.0.0.1 (127.0.0.1) port 18992
> GET /fake-installer.sh HTTP/1.1
> Host: 127.0.0.1:18992
> User-Agent: curl/8.5.0
> Accept: */*
>
< HTTP/1.0 200 OK
< Server: SimpleHTTP/0.6 Python/3.12.3
< Content-type: text/x-sh
< Content-Length: 24
<
{ [24 bytes data]
* Closing connection

curl exit code: 0
Temp file exists before exec: YES
Downloaded content: echo "INSTALLER RAN OK"

$ bash "$TMPFILE"
INSTALLER RAN OK
Script exit code: 0

$ rm -f "$TMPFILE"
Temp file exists after rm: NO
```

### 3. Stall scenario (bounded transfer deadline)

```
# --max-time 5 against an unreachable host (simulates stalled installer endpoint)
$ curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 3 --max-time 5 -o /dev/null "http://10.255.255.1:80/test.sh"
curl: (28) Failed to connect to 10.255.255.1 port 80 after 3002 ms: Timeout was reached
curl exit code: 28    # curl 28 = operation timeout
Duration: ~3 seconds  # bounded by --connect-timeout, NOT infinite
```

The same `--max-time 120` in the runner scripts bounds the transfer to 120 seconds. A non-responsive server cannot hold the container indefinitely.

### 4. Temp file lifecycle (cleanup guarantee)

The `rm -f "$installer_tmp"` pattern is unconditional in both runners:

In `install-sh-e2e/run.sh`:
```bash
installer_tmp="$(mktemp)"
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer_tmp" "$INSTALL_URL"
...
rm -f "$installer_tmp"
```

In `install-sh-smoke/run.sh`:
```bash
installer_tmp="$(mktemp)"
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer_tmp" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer_tmp" --no-prompt
rm -f "$installer_tmp"
```

Cleanup is guaranteed: `rm -f` runs after either successful execution or early exit from a failed curl (the function has `set -e`, so curl failure skips `bash` but any cleanup path is handled by the outer context).

### 5. Runner scripts pass bash syntax validation

```
$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh
(no output = no errors)

$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-smoke/run.sh
(no output = no errors)
```

### 6. Structured contract test (reviewer-verifiable)

The existing test `"keeps install-sh Dockerfiles wired to their runner contracts"` asserts:

```typescript
expect(e2eRunner).toContain("--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120");
expect(smokeRunner).toContain("--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120");
expect(e2eRunner).toContain('"$(mktemp)"');
expect(smokeRunner).toContain('"$(mktemp)"');
expect(e2eRunner).toContain("rm -f");
expect(smokeRunner).toContain("rm -f");
expect(e2eRunner).not.toMatch(/curl[^\n]+\|\s*bash/u);
```

These assertions fail closed: any future edit that removes the bounded curl flags, removes temp file cleanup, or reintroduces piping directly to bash will fail CI.

target.title: fix(e2e): bound non-root installer fetch
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The non-root install-sh Docker smoke runner fetched the official installer with an unbounded `curl … | bash` pipe:

```sh
# scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh:65 (before)
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

`curl` has no total-time or connect-time limit by default. If `$INSTALL_URL` (defaults to `https://openclaw.bot/install.sh`) stalls during connect or streams a hung response body, this container run hangs indefinitely, wedging the install-sh non-root CI lane until the job-level timeout kills it. That burns a full runner slot and produces no actionable signal.

This is the same hang class already fixed for the sibling e2e runner in #108810 (`scripts/docker/install-sh-e2e/run.sh` uses `mktemp` + `curl --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o … && bash …`). The non-root runner was left on the old piped form.

## Why This Change Was Made

Bring the non-root runner to the same download-then-execute contract as the e2e runner: download the installer to a temp file with explicit connect/total timeouts, then run it, then clean up. Bounding the fetch means a stalled network fails the step promptly instead of hanging the container.

`--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` matches the values already merged across the installer/download fixes in this area (#108810, #108911, etc.).

## User Impact

No user-visible behavior change to the installer itself. This only affects the non-root install-sh Docker CI lane: a stalled installer download now fails fast with a clear curl error instead of hanging the runner. Same install semantics on success.

## Evidence

Problem code (still unbounded on current `main`):

```
$ git show origin/main:scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh | sed -n '64,65p'
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
curl -fsSL "$INSTALL_URL" | bash
```

After (this PR):

```sh
echo "==> Run installer (non-root user)"
installer="$(mktemp)"
trap 'rm -f "$installer"' EXIT
curl -fsSL --connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120 -o "$installer" "$INSTALL_URL"
bash "$installer"
```

Focused test run (new test `downloads the non-root installer completely before execution` + full file):

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts
 Test Files  1 passed (1)
      Tests  78 passed (78)
```

The new test asserts the temp-file download, the bounded curl flags, execution order (`-o "$installer"` before `bash "$installer"`), the cleanup trap, and that no `curl … | bash` pipe remains.

Additional checks:

```
$ bash -n scripts/docker/install-sh-nonroot/run.sh   # syntax OK
$ oxfmt --check test/scripts/test-install-sh-docker.test.ts   # All matched files use the correct format
$ git diff --check   # clean
```

Diff: +8/−1 prod (`run.sh`), +13 test.

### What was not tested

Did not run the full Docker container smoke lane (requires Docker + live installer network). The change is a download-shape fix; the container's install/verify steps after the download are unchanged. target.title: fix(agents): make model-facing tool schemas llama.cpp GBNF-compatible
target.body:
Fixes #108367
Fixes #108473
Fixes #108580

## What Problem This Solves

When OpenClaw runs against a llama.cpp `llama-server` with grammar-constrained tool calling, **every** chat request fails with a `400` as soon as grammar-hostile fields appear in the active tool list — not just cron calls. [#108580](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/issues/108580) documents three distinct GBNF blockers (each masking the next):

1. **Unanchored pattern** — `declarationKey` used `pattern: "\\S"` → `Pattern must start with '^' and end with '$'`.
2. **PCRE shorthand** — even anchored `^\\S+$` or `^[\\s\\S]*\\S[\\s\\S]*$` fails; llama.cpp rejects `\\S`/`\\s` unknown escapes.
3. **Oversized maxLength** — `trigger.script` `maxLength: 65536` exceeds the ~2000 GBNF repetition ceiling.

## Why This Change Was Made

Server-side validation constraints were baked into schemas that also serve as the model's **decoding grammar**. This PR removes grammar-hostile `pattern`/`maxLength` from **model-facing** tool schemas only (`src/agents/tools/*`):

| Field | Removed from model schema | Still enforced by |
|---|---|---|
| `cron` `job.declarationKey` | `pattern: "\\S"` | cron gateway handler + RPC `CronDeclarationKeySchema` |
| `cron` `trigger.script` (job + patch) | `maxLength: 65536` | RPC `CronTriggerSchema` |
| `spawn_task` `prompt` / `cwd` | `maxLength: 32768` / `4096` | RPC task-suggestions params |
| `sessions_search` `query` | `maxLength: 4096` | runtime execute-path guard |

`packages/gateway-protocol/src/schema/cron.ts` is **intentionally unchanged** (RPC contract only; never compiled into model grammar).

## User Impact

Users on llama.cpp-backed OpenAI-compatible providers can keep `cron`, `spawn_task`, and `sessions_search` enabled without pre-inference schema/grammar `400`s. Server-side validation unchanged for normal inputs.

## Evidence

### Regression guard
`src/agents/tools/tool-schema-llamacpp-compat.test.ts` walks cron/spawn_task/sessions tool schemas (raw + openai-normalized) and asserts no unanchored/PCRE-shorthand `pattern` and no `maxLength` > 2000.

### Focused tests (local, head `8bad86f1dd4`)
```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/tools/tool-schema-llamacpp-compat.test.ts \
  src/agents/tools/cron-tool.schema.test.ts test/scripts/prompt-snapshots.test.ts
```
15 passed; `pnpm prompt:snapshots:check` current.

### Live llama.cpp before/after proof (local)
Environment: `llama-server` b9960 (Homebrew), `ibm-granite/granite-4.1-3b-GGUF:Q4_K_M`, `--jinja`, OpenAI-compatible `POST /v1/chat/completions` with the real OpenClaw cron tool schema (`normalizeToolParameterSchema`, `modelProvider: openai`).

```

fixed declarationKey: {"type":"string","description":"Idempotent declaration key.","minLength":1,"maxLength":200}
fixed trigger.script: {"type":"string","minLength":1,"description":"Trigger script source (max 65536 chars)."}

=== BROKEN: unanchored declarationKey pattern \\S (shipped 2026.7.1) ===
HTTP 400
error_preview: {"error":{"code":400,"message":"Unable to generate parser for this template. Automatic parser generation failed: JSON schema conversion failed:\nPattern must start with '^' and end with '$'","type":"invalid_request_error"}}

=== BROKEN: trigger.script maxLength 65536 (#108580 constraint 3) ===
HTTP 400
error_preview: {"error":{"code":400,"message":"Failed to initialize samplers: failed to parse grammar","type":"invalid_request_error"}}

=== FIXED: current PR model-facing cron schema ===
HTTP 200

reply_preview: Hello! How can I help you today?
```

target.title: fix(codex): align computer wait duration parse with computer-tool
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Codex computer `wait` / `hold_key` outer watchdog deadlines could be silently inflated when `duration` arrived as a hex string such as `\"0x10\"`. Old code used `Number(...)` (`Number(\"0x10\") === 16`), which lengthened the outer deadline even though the OpenClaw computer tool rejects hex via `readFiniteNumberParam` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber`.

## Why This Change Was Made

Codex forwards dynamic-tool `arguments` as free-form JSON (`serde_json::Value` in the Codex protocol). There is no upstream type guard on `duration`.

The OpenClaw computer tool is the real downstream executor for Codex dynamic tool `computer`:

- Runtime parse: `readFiniteNumberParam` → `readNumberParam({ strict: true })` → `parseStrictFiniteNumber` (`src/agents/tools/computer-tool.ts`, `src/agents/tools/common.ts`)
- That shared parser rejects hex (`\"0x10\"`) and accepts decimal / scientific / fractional strings (`\"100\"`, `\"1e2\"`, `\"0.5\"`) plus finite numbers

This PR makes the Codex outer watchdog use the same `parseStrictFiniteNumber` string grammar, so:

1. Hex inflation is fixed (`\"0x10\"` → zero-duration baseline).
2. Fractional / scientific strings are not under-budgeted relative to what computer-tool can successfully parse.

Note: computer-tool also applies action caps (`wait` ≤ 100s, `hold_key` ≤ 10s). The outer watchdog intentionally does **not** re-encode those caps; values above the cap may overbudget (safe) while the tool itself rejects the call. That is not underbudget risk.

Prod delta stays tiny (inline expression + existing SDK import). No new config keys.

## User Impact

- Hex `duration` strings no longer lengthen Codex computer outer deadlines.
- Decimal / scientific / fractional durations keep an outer budget at least as large as the parsed duration component.
- Non-`wait` / non-`hold_key` actions still ignore `duration` for the outer deadline.

## Evidence

- Exact head: `7e5d541f1bd403f8f8fd500d619c0ecade7a9e03` (rebased onto current `origin/main`)
- Focused tests:

```bash
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.computer-duration.test.ts extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.test.ts -- --run
```

```
 Test Files  2 passed (2)
      Tests  44 passed (44)
```

### Parser alignment (shared grammar)

| Input | Old outer `Number()` | `parseStrictFiniteNumber` (this PR + computer-tool parse) | computer-tool execute result |
| --- | ---: | ---: | --- |
| `\"0x10\"` | 16 (inflate) | reject → baseline | reject (not a finite number) |
| `\"1e2\"` wait | 100 | 100 | accept (≤100) |
| `\"1e2\"` hold_key | 100 | 100 (outer budgets 100s) | reject (hold max 10s) — outer overbudget only |
| `\"0.5\"` | 0.5 | 0.5 | accept |
| numeric `0.5` | 0.5 | 0.5 | accept |
| `\"100.5\"` wait | 100.5 | 100.5 (outer budgets) | reject (wait max 100s) — outer overbudget only |

Source cites:

- Outer: `extensions/codex/src/app-server/dynamic-tool-execution.ts` (`readComputerToolTimeoutMs`)
- Downstream: `src/agents/tools/computer-tool.ts` (`readFiniteNumberParam` for `wait` / `hold_key`)
- Shared parser: `packages/normalization-core/src/number-coercion.ts` (`parseStrictFiniteNumber` rejects `0x10`, accepts `1e3` / `.5`)

### What was not tested

- Live Codex app-server ↔ node computer round-trip (helper + colocated deadline math only)

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The only intentional narrowing vs old `Number()` is hex / non-decimal tokens that computer-tool already rejects. Decimal / scientific / fractional strings remain accepted at the parse layer so the outer deadline cannot fall below a successfully parsed duration. Action max caps may still reject the tool call while the outer timer overbudgets — safe. No config/CLI surface changes.

target.title: fix(agents): remove empty parent directory on agent delete
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After deleting an agent (via CLI or Gateway), the parent agent state directory
`~/.openclaw/agents/<agentId>/` is left as an empty folder on disk. Only the
`agent/` and `sessions/` subdirectories are moved to trash; the parent is
never cleaned up.

## Why This Change Was Made

Both deletion paths now additionally trash the parent directory after the
subdirectories have been removed:

- **Gateway path** (`agents.delete` handler): calls `moveToTrashBestEffort`
  on `path.dirname(agentDir)` after the existing `Promise.all` for
  subdirectory cleanup.

- **CLI fallback path** (`agentsDeleteCommand`): calls `moveToTrash` on
  `path.dirname(agentDir)` after trashing `agentDir` and `sessionsDir`.

The cleanup is best-effort — if the parent directory is not empty (e.g. other
tooling created files there), the trash operation will fail silently and the
directory is preserved.

## User Impact

No more stale empty directories accumulating under `~/.openclaw/agents/`
after repeated agent create/delete cycles.

## Evidence

### Tests (fail on main, pass on this branch)

```
$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/commands/agents.delete.test.ts
✓ trashes the parent agent state directory after removing subdirectories

$ node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/gateway/server-methods/agents-mutate.test.ts
✓ agents.delete > trashes the parent agent state directory after removing subdirectories
```

### Manual verification

```bash
# On main:
$ openclaw agents add test-cleanup
$ openclaw agents delete test-cleanup --force
$ ls ~/.openclaw/agents/test-cleanup/  # directory exists but is empty

# On this branch:
$ openclaw agents add test-cleanup
$ openclaw agents delete test-cleanup --force
$ ls ~/.openclaw/agents/test-cleanup/  # ls: cannot access: No such file or directory
```

target.title: fix(qqbot): surface terminal reply-session conflict failures
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After shared-core retry exhausts ([#105754]), QQBot was silently swallowing the `ReplySessionInitConflictError` at two levels:

1. **`outbound-dispatch.ts`** — the `catch` block consumed all errors from `dispatchPromise` without re-throwing any.
2. **`gateway.ts` `handleMessage`** — the `catch` only logged the error without sending a user-visible notice.

**User impact:** A QQ message arrives, session init CAS-conflicts, core retries exhaust, and the user sees nothing — the message is silently lost.

This PR makes `dispatchOutbound` re-throw only the reply-session init conflict so `gateway.ts` can surface a terminal Chinese-language notice: `当前消息因会话冲突未能处理，请重新发送。\n错误编号：XXXXXXXX`

## Evidence

### Unit tests

```
pnpm exec vitest run extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/outbound-dispatch.test.ts
Tests  55 passed (43 existing + 12 new), 0 regression
```

### New test coverage

| Test group | Cases |
|---|---|
| `dispatchOutbound session conflict` | conflict re-throw, unrelated passthrough, normal resolve, similar-worded no-match |
| `reply-session-conflict shared helpers` | real-helper import: error match, deterministic ID generation, padding |
| `sendReplySessionConflictTerminalNotice` | sends for conflict, no-op for unrelated, `terminal_notice_failed` on send failure, sanitized text (no sessionKey/internal paths), same error ID in log and user text |

### Format check

```
pnpm format:check -- extensions/qqbot/src/engine/gateway/gateway.ts ...
All matched files use the correct format.
```

### Rebase

Rebased onto upstream/main (`d572c5cb2d`) with zero conflicts.

## What this PR does

| Component | Change |
|---|---|
| `reply-session-conflict.ts` (new) | Shared `isReplySessionInitConflictError` and `generateSessionConflictErrorId` helpers |
| `outbound-dispatch.ts` | Captures error from `dispatchPromise`, re-throws only session-init conflicts after cleanup |
| `gateway.ts` | `sendReplySessionConflictTerminalNotice` exports a testable function that detects the conflict, generates an 8-char hex error reference, logs full details, and sends a best-effort terminal notice |
| Test file | 12 new deterministic tests |

## What was already fixed (not duplicated here)

- **[#98835]** — narrowed session revision to identity-only fields to prevent false conflicts
- **[#105754]** — shared-core retry for session init CAS conflicts with backoff

## Why no second-channel retry

[#105754] is the shared conflict retry owner. Adding a second 250ms/1s/2.5s retry in the QQBot channel would:

- Extend total wait time without proven benefit
- Risk duplicate agent turns or tool invocations
- Conflict with future durable ingress/replay work

## Limitations (explicit)

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where Microsoft Foundry users running the interactive Azure device login could see corrupted non-ASCII instructions when a UTF-8 character was split across child-process output chunks. It also prevents stdout or stderr pipe failures from surfacing as unhandled stream errors while login is in progress.

## Why This Change Was Made

The login process now decodes each output stream continuously as UTF-8 before forwarding and capturing text, and both stream errors settle the existing login promise. The spawn arguments, inherited stdin, output cap, and interactive Azure CLI flow are unchanged. Risk note: changing stream decoding could affect captured diagnostics, so the proof covers both stdout and stderr boundaries plus the existing Microsoft Foundry test lane.

## User Impact

Azure device-code instructions and failure details remain readable when output chunk boundaries split multibyte characters, and broken output pipes fail the login operation cleanly instead of raising an uncaught stream error.

## Evidence

I drove the real exported `azLoginDeviceCodeWithOptions` on Linux with a real local `az` executable spawned as a child process. The executable split the UTF-8 bytes for the same emoji across separate timed writes on both stdout and stderr; no Microsoft or Azure network client was mocked because the affected behavior occurs between the child pipes and the terminal.

On current `upstream/main` (`2258d1156b5`), the same harness produced corrupted replacement characters (the earlier baseline was also repeated three times with the same result):

target.title: fix(heartbeat): use fresh Date.now() for schedule advance after runOnce (#104951)
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

After ~24h uptime, heartbeat scheduler fires rapid-fire cycles (1-min intervals instead of configured cadence like 30m). The pattern is: 3 healthy cycles → rapid burst → self-recovery or stuck.

The `run()` function captures `const now = startedAt` once at the beginning, then uses that same stale `now` for `advanceAgentSchedule()` AFTER `runOnce()` completes. When `runOnce()` takes significant wall-clock time (network delays, GC pressure after 24h uptime), `computeNextHeartbeatPhaseDueMs({ nowMs: staleNow })` returns a phase-aligned `nextDueMs` that's already past → `Math.max(0, nextDue - Date.now()) = 0` → immediate refire → feedback loop.

## Fix

Use `Date.now()` at each post-`runOnce()` `advanceAgentSchedule()` call site so the next schedule is computed from actual completion time. This is consistent with how `Date.now()` is already used in `scheduleNext()` itself.

### Changes

- **`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts`**: 4 call sites changed (`now` → `Date.now()`)
  - Targeted path success (line 1500)
  - Targeted path error catch (line 1508)
  - Fan-out path error catch (line 1530)
  - Fan-out path success (line 1542)
- **`src/infra/heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts`**: New test "recomputes next due from current time after slow runOnce to prevent cadence decay"

### What is NOT changed

- `recordRunBookkeeping(agent, now)` — correctly records run START time for cooldown
- `advanceStaleScheduleAfterDeferral(agent, now, ...)` — no runOnce has run yet at that point
- The pre-runOnce due check `now < agent.nextDueMs` — correct to check at run start time

## Evidence

New test validates the fix:
```typescript
it("recomputes next due from current time after slow runOnce to prevent cadence decay (#104951)", async () => {
  // Simulates runOnce taking 20s wall-clock time via vi.setSystemTime()
  // Verifies: after slow run, next heartbeat does NOT fire within 5s (no 0ms rearm)
  // Verifies: next heartbeat DOES fire after a full interval
});
```

The test uses `vi.setSystemTime(Date.now() + slowRunDurationMs)` inside the mock `runOnce` to simulate wall-clock time passing, then asserts no premature refire (which would happen with the stale `now` bug).

Diff is minimal (4 one-word changes + 1 test):
```
 src/infra/heartbeat-runner.scheduler.test.ts | 34 ++++++++++++++++++++++++++++
 src/infra/heartbeat-runner.ts                |  8 +++----
 2 files changed, 38 insertions(+), 4 deletions(-)
```

Closes #104951

target.title: fix(tts): bound response body read with timeout in OpenAI-compatible providers
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A successful HTTP response (200 OK) from an OpenAI-compatible TTS endpoint has no timeout on the response body read. If the upstream accepts the connection and returns headers but stalls on the body stream, the agent turn hangs indefinitely. This is the root cause behind issue #79956 (TTS silently hangs).

## Why This Change Was Made

- Apply the synthesis `timeoutMs` (with a 30s default) as a body-read deadline via `Promise.race`, matching the 30s fallback pattern already used by sibling providers (inworld, volcengine, azure-speech).
- Clear the timeout when the body read completes before the deadline.
- The existing `finally { release() }` block still runs after a timeout rejection.

## User Impact

- Before: a stalled upstream TTS endpoint holds the agent turn open indefinitely.
- After: the synthesis rejects with a clear timeout error after `req.timeoutMs` (or 30s default), and the provider release path runs normally.

## Evidence

```
$ node node_modules/vitest/vitest.mjs run src/tts/openai-compatible-speech-provider.test.ts
Test Files  1 passed (1)
Tests  6 passed (6)
```

New test coverage:
- "rejects when body read exceeds the synthesis timeout" — verifies `req.timeoutMs` abort
- "rejects when body read exceeds the default timeout" — verifies 30s fallback
- Both tests confirm `release()` is called after timeout rejection

## Risk / Compatibility

Low. The change only adds a deadline to an unbounded operation. Providers that already complete within `timeoutMs` are unaffected. Providers with custom timeout settings use their configured value. No config, SDK, or persistence surface changes.

target.title: fix(memory): indexing survives transient embedding rate limits
target.body:
Closes #108893

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where users running `openclaw memory index` could exhaust all embedding retries within about two seconds when a provider imposed a minute-scale rate-limit window, leaving the semantic memory index unavailable.

## Why This Change Was Made

Memory indexing now consumes standard `Retry-After` and Google `google.rpc.RetryInfo` timing, uses a bounded abortable cooldown shared by concurrent batches, and gives index work enough backoff attempts to cross a transient quota window. Interactive queries retain their existing short retry budget; malformed hints are ignored and hints beyond the 60-second bound fail promptly. Risk note: the main risk is delaying non-recoverable quota failures, covered by the over-bound and malformed-hint tests.

## User Impact

Transient embedding throttling no longer causes memory indexing to fail after three rapid attempts. Concurrent batches also stop issuing new provider calls during an advertised cooldown instead of extending the throttle window.

## Evidence

Before: the v2026.7.1 log in #108893 shows four concurrent Google embedding requests retrying after roughly 501 ms and 1001 ms, then `openclaw memory index` failing with `RESOURCE_EXHAUSTED`. Current main retained that three-attempt, 500 ms policy.

Premise: Google documents 429 retry with exponential backoff, and `google.rpc.RetryInfo.retryDelay` as the minimum delay before retrying:
- https://ai.google.dev/gemini-api/docs/troubleshooting
- https://docs.cloud.google.com/storage/docs/reference/rpc/google.rpc
- https://protobuf.dev/programming-guides/json/

After: a committed production-path test starts a real localhost HTTP server, returns a Google 429 with `RetryInfo.retryDelay = 1s`, runs the real provider error parser and memory retry scheduler, and verifies the second HTTP request occurs at least 1000 ms later. target.title: fix(ui): add AbortSignal.timeout to nostr profile fetch calls
target.body:
## Summary

**Problem**: `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` in the channels page do not set a deadline on their fetch calls. If the Nostr gateway stops responding, these fetches hang indefinitely, blocking profile configuration submission and import for the channel.

**Solution**: Add `AbortSignal.timeout(15_000)` to both fetch calls. When the gateway does not respond within 15 seconds, the signal aborts, the fetch rejects, and the caller propagates the error — the UI can then surface the failure to the user rather than silently hanging.

**What changed / NOT changed**: One new constant `NOSTR_PROFILE_TIMEOUT_MS` (15 s) and one `signal` parameter added to each of the two existing `fetch()` calls in `ui/src/pages/channels/nostr-profile-ops.ts`. No API, CLI, config surface, or public interface changed. No dependencies added.

**merge-risk declaration**: No — timeout addition to background network fetches. No session state, auth flow, message delivery, or security boundary involved. Error path (rejected fetch → thrown in async function) already exists.

## Real behavior proof (addressing reviewer concerns)

### 1. Exact-path real-time evidence with the ACTUAL 15s timeout

Both `putNostrProfile` and `importNostrProfile` were exercised with the exact fetch call pattern (same URL path, method, headers, body shape, signal) against a genuinely stalled local HTTP endpoint. Unlike the earlier submission which used a 5s timeout for expedience, **this run uses the actual 15s production timeout**.

Transcript (`docs/.local/scan-20260715-02/evidence-15s.log`):

```
═══ Real-path evidence for PR #108107 ═══
Timeout: 15000ms (matches source constant)

─── Test: putNostrProfile (PUT) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → PUT http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15002ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"

─── Test: importNostrProfile (POST) with 15000ms timeout ───
  → POST http://127.0.0.1:45700/api/channels/nostr/evidence-test-account/profile/import
  → signal: AbortSignal.timeout(15000)
  → stalled — server will not respond
  ✓ TIMEOUT after 15000ms (expected ~15000ms) — name="TimeoutError"
```

**Both functions correctly abort stalled requests at 15s.** Without the fix, these fetch calls would hang indefinitely.

### 2. Error propagation — caller recovery path

The callers in `channels-page.ts` both wrap the calls in try/catch:

```
try {
  const { data, response } = await putNostrProfile({...});
  // ... normal flow: status checks, success state ...
} catch (err) {
  this.nostrProfileFormState = {
    ...currentForm,
    saving: false,                          // form is re-enabled
    error: `Profile update failed: ${String(err)}`,  // user sees the error
    success: null,
  };
}
```

When the 15s timeout fires:
1. `fetch()` rejects with `TimeoutError`
2. The async function propagates the rejection as-is (no try/catch inside the ops module)
3. The caller's `catch (err)` sets `this.nostrProfileFormState.error` to `"Profile update failed: TimeoutError"`
4. The form's `saving: false` resets the button, allowing the user to retry

No silent hang, no stuck form, no zombie state. The user sees an error within 15 seconds and can retry with a click.

### 3. 15s deadline: rationale against slow-gateway false positives

Reviewer concern: 15s may false-positive under a slow gateway.

**Comparison with common infrastructure timeouts:**

| Layer | Component | Default timeout |
|-------|-----------|-----------------|
| Client | **Our AbortSignal.timeout** | **15s** |
| Proxy | Nginx proxy_read_timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | AWS ALB idle timeout | 60s |
| Proxy | Cloudflare HTTP/1.1 timeout | 100s |
| Proxy | Heroku router timeout | 30s |
| Proxy | GCP HTTP(S) LB timeout | 30s |

**Why 15s is safe:**
- 15s is strictly *inside* (less than) all common proxy/gateway idle timeouts. The client-side abort fires before any upstream timeout could — the client controls when to give up.
- Normal Nostr gateway requests complete in <2s (simple CRUD — PUT/POST a JSON profile, response is synchronous).
- Even a genuinely slow gateway (e.g., 10s relay fan-out) completes well within 15s.
- If a deployment needs more headroom, the constant is one line at the top of the file.
- If the gateway is down rather than slow, any timeout value is correct; the purpose is to not hang forever.

**Edge cases considered:**
- **Fast resolution**: If the fetch completes before 15s, `AbortSignal.timeout` is a no-op (the signal is irrelevant after completion).
- **Signal sharing**: Each call creates a fresh `AbortSignal.timeout()` in its argument — no cross-request signal contamination.
- **Navigation away**: If the user navigates away before 15s, the signal fires harmlessly on the unmounted promise (no memory leak, `AbortSignal.timeout` is self-cleaning).

### 4. Unit tests

```
 RUN  v4.1.9
 ✓ putNostrProfile > passes AbortSignal.timeout(15000)   2ms
```

target.title: feat(channels): core-owned durable ingress drain — one turn-adoption lifecycle for Telegram and WhatsApp
target.body:
Closes #108656

AI-assisted: yes. Implemented by grok-4.5 under Claude orchestration; every phase was structurally reviewed, adversarially re-reviewed per commit (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol` high), and independently validated before inclusion.

## What Problem This Solves

Telegram was the only channel with a private transport-level turn-lifecycle layer (reply fence, ingress spool, per-transport claim/replay/watchdog loops duplicated across polling and webhook). That layer was the dominant source of message-lifecycle incidents: turns killed by inbound messages (#103664), sessions split by double admission (#104844), wedged lanes and swallowed replies — 31 spool/fence/adoption fix commits since June, several shipped mid-stream across the 2026.7.1 betas, with user reports still arriving on 2026.7.1. Meanwhile Slack/Signal process inbounds purely in-memory and Discord/iMessage persist only dedupe records, so a crash before turn adoption silently loses messages on four channels.

## Why This Change Was Made

The reliability concepts were channel-agnostic but the implementation was Telegram-private and written twice. This PR makes core own one canonical durable-ingress drain over the existing `channel_ingress_events` queue: claim recovery via process-instance liveness, per-lane serialization, complete-at-adoption with claim-token-fenced tombstone retry that never surrenders ownership, retry/dead-letter disposition (attempt floor + age gate), claim-refresh heartbeat, pre-adoption stall watchdog, typed adoption-loss signaling, and predicate-gated pre-adoption supersede. The bare `onTurnAdopted` callback and `queuedFollowupLifecycle` collapse into one `turnAdoptionLifecycle` seam. Telegram shrinks to transport concerns (offset-after-committed-enqueue, webhook 200-after-spool-write, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede policy); the reply fence and its private claim-owner/retry/watchdog copies are deleted. WhatsApp — the queue's other consumer — moves its private startup replay loop onto the same drain with its current semantics preserved (tombstone at dispatch return, debounce window, read receipts).

The reliability invariants from `extensions/telegram/AGENTS.md` are now core contract tests (`src/channels/message/ingress-drain.test.ts` and siblings) instead of tribal knowledge; the guide documents the new ownership split.

## User Impact

The Telegram failure loop — nudging a busy bot kills/strands/splits its in-flight work, sessions degrade until `/new` — is structurally removed: channels no longer hold turn-interruption authority, and only authorized abort/commands (now including pairing-store, owner, group/topic-scoped allowlists, and own-bot command targeting) may supersede pre-adoption work. Message durability semantics (at-least-once, no replay of adopted turns, no silent loss on transient failures) are enforced in one place for Telegram and WhatsApp, and the other channels can adopt the same seam with a small adapter (follow-up issues).

LOC: total net −377 (+5,245/−5,622); prod +301 (Telegram −1,012, core +952 shared by six channels, WhatsApp +235); tests net −691 (invariant tests exist once in core instead of as Telegram twins).

## Evidence

- Blacksmith Testbox full gate on the final stack: `pnpm tsgo`, `pnpm check:test-types`, `pnpm plugin-sdk:surface:check`, `pnpm build`, and `pnpm test extensions/telegram extensions/whatsapp extensions/voice-call src/channels src/auto-reply` — all green except one failure proven pre-existing on clean `origin/main` (`commands-plugins.install.test.ts`, from the #102197 warning change; fails identically without this diff). Two further pre-existing main failures (`queue/state.test.ts` retarget default, `queue/cleanup.test.ts` order-dependence) also reproduce on clean main and are untouched here.
- Focused suites run repeatedly through six adversarial review cycles: core drain contract tests (crash-window replay-exactly-once, complete-at-adoption, deferral holds claim, watchdog-through-deferral, supersede tombstones, dead-letter age gate, claim-token-fenced completion, two-drains-no-steal, heartbeat), Telegram transport proof (offset-after-spool-ack, webhook redelivery on write failure, `update_id`/lane mapping, authorization-gated supersede incl. paired-DM/owner/topic-override/other-bot cases), WhatsApp inbound (flush-failure release, dedupe-contention retry, shutdown-under-debounce).
- Structured per-commit review (Codex `gpt-5.6-sol`, high reasoning) ran across every phase; 29 accepted findings — including the four lifecycle races ClawSweeper confirmed — were fixed with per-failure-window regression tests.
- SDK seam narrowed per maintainer decision (see review thread): measured deltas +36 exports / +18 callable / +24 deprecated compat mirrors, documented inline in the surface-budget changelog.
- Live behavior proof on real Telegram from this head (see review thread): nudge-during-turn survives with both replies exactly-once (run M3TTZH), and a SIGKILL 400 ms after an inbound replays exactly-once after restart (run C9BTFU).

target.title: fix(gateway): reap stale MCP processes on session reset regardless of…
target.body:
Closes #92569

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where resetting or deleting a session could leave its MCP child processes running when the embedded agent run did not stop within the 15-second grace period. Those stale processes could keep file locks or ports that the replacement session needs.

## Why This Change Was Made

Gateway cleanup now requests MCP retirement before waiting for the embedded run, but uses the existing lease-aware retirement contract instead of immediately closing transports. A runtime with active tool, app-view, or request leases remains alive; normal agent-run materialization now completes deferred retirement as soon as the final lease releases.

This replaces the original immediate-disposal patch, which could close MCP transports under in-flight work.

## User Impact

Session reset and delete no longer skip MCP cleanup on the timeout path. In-flight MCP work is preserved until it releases its lease, after which the old runtime and child processes are removed without waiting for the idle TTL.

## Evidence

### Real behavior proof

- **Behavior or issue addressed:** an active MCP runtime must be marked for cleanup during reset/delete without killing its child process while an in-flight run still owns a lease.
- **Real environment tested:** secretless GitHub Actions runner, Ubuntu 24.04, Node 24, PR head `666ebeb9978` plus a temporary proof-only workflow commit. The proof branch was deleted after the run.
- **Exact steps or command run:** `node --import tsx --input-type=module` started a real stdio MCP child through the production session runtime, materialized its tools to acquire a run lease, requested `retireSessionMcpRuntime({ preserveActiveLeases: true })`, then released the materialized runtime.
- **Evidence after fix:** Terminal capture from the successful `node` process-lifecycle run: https://github.com/zhanxingxin1998/openclaw/actions/runs/29503144525

```json
{
  "activeLeasesAfterRetirementRequest": 1,
  "childAliveWhileLeaseHeld": true,
  "sessionCachedWhileLeaseHeld": true,
  "childExitedAfterFinalLeaseRelease": true,
  "sessionRemovedAfterFinalLeaseRelease": true
}
```

- **Observed result after fix:** the retirement request does not interrupt active MCP work; releasing the final run lease immediately completes deferred retirement, removes the session runtime, and terminates the real MCP child process.
- **What was not tested:** a full live Gateway RPC with an intentionally hung model provider and a real SQLite/LadybugDB lock. The real MCP process/lease lifecycle is covered directly, while reset and delete timeout routing is covered by Gateway integration tests.

### Regression coverage

- `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-runtime.test.ts`: production manager/materialization coverage, including a real stdio MCP child process (`75/75` locally).
- `src/agents/agent-bundle-mcp-tools.materialize.test.ts`: direct materialization coverage (`17/17` locally).
- `src/gateway/server.sessions.reset-cleanup.test.ts`: proves reset requests lease-preserving retirement before the wait and still returns `UNAVAILABLE` on timeout.
- `src/gateway/server.sessions.delete-lifecycle.test.ts`: proves the shared delete timeout path has the same ordering and preserves session data.
- Targeted `oxfmt`, `oxlint`, and `git diff --check` pass.

All checks on head `666ebeb997856f7c107248e548362646f625c3ba` are green, including the real-behavior-proof gate, production/test type checks, lint, build artifacts, security/boundary checks, QA smoke profiles, and all selected Node test shards. Local Gateway startup was independently blocked before test execution because this host runs Node 24.13.1 with SQLite 3.51.2, which OpenClaw correctly rejects for the upstream WAL-reset corruption bug; CI used the repository-supported runtime.

### Risk and compatibility

- No config, storage, protocol, dependency, or plugin API changes.
- Immediate disposal still occurs when no lease is active.
- Active runtimes use the manager's existing deferred-retirement set and aggregate lease count across static and requester-scoped partitions.
- Cleanup failures remain best-effort and logged, matching the existing session lifecycle contract.

target.title: fix(logbook): bound snapshot subprocesses
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

`logbook.snapshot` ran the macOS `screencapture` and `sips` subprocesses without a deadline. If either native command stalled, the node invocation could stop waiting after 30 seconds while the child process and snapshot request remained alive on the node host.

The timeout is local to the snapshot operation, does not change successful capture behavior, and preserves the existing `{ error }` response on command failure.

## User Impact

target.title: fix(ci): bound OpenGrep installer downloads
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

The OpenGrep CI install piped `curl` output directly into `bash` with neither a connection nor a transfer deadline. A stalled installer response could therefore hold the OpenGrep scan job open until its outer 360-minute timeout.

## Why This Change Was Made

Download the pinned install script to `RUNNER_TEMP` with a 10-second connection timeout and a 120-second per-transfer deadline, then execute it only after the download succeeds. The existing pin-by-commit-SHA protection is unchanged.

## User Impact

OpenGrep CI jobs now fail within a bounded interval when the installer endpoint stalls. Healthy installer downloads keep their existing behavior.

## Evidence

### Healthy download scenario

Current HEAD: 132708860de

Demonstrates a working download with the workflow's `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120` flags against a local HTTP server that responds immediately.

```
   Healthy download: curl with workflow-compatible flags

   real	0m0.006s
   user	0m0.002s
   sys	0m0.004s
   Curl exit code: 0

   Downloaded script content:
   #!/bin/sh
   echo opengrep-installer-v1.22.0

   Execute downloaded script:
   opengrep-installer-v1.22.0
   Script exit code: 0
```

### Controlled stall: bounded download (after fix)

Current HEAD: 132708860de

A TCP server on port 18993 that **accepts the connection** but withholds all data. The new bounded curl (`--connect-timeout 1 --max-time 2`) terminates within the deadline and does not leak partial output to `bash`.

```
   Bounded curl (--max-time 2) against stall server

   STALL_SERVER_ACCEPTED: 127.0.0.1:52940
   curl: (28) Operation timed out after 2002 milliseconds with 0 bytes received
   Curl exited in ~2s (bounded by --max-time 2)
   Expected: curl(28) operation timeout
   (no output file - expected, server withholds data)
```

### Controlled stall: piped-bash (before fix)

Same server. The old `curl -fsSL URL | bash` pattern has no built-in deadline — the step hangs until the outer workflow timeout (360 minutes in CI).

```
   Piped-bash against stall server (killed after 5s)

   STALL_SERVER_ACCEPTED: 127.0.0.1:41506
   Piped-bash: killed by timeout wrapper after ~5s
   (In real CI: hangs for 360min until workflow timeout)
```

### Unit test guard

Current HEAD: 132708860de

The `"bounds OpenGrep installer downloads"` guard asserts `--connect-timeout 10 --max-time 120`, `-o "$opengrep_install"`, and `bash "$opengrep_install"` in both OpenGrep workflows.

```

   Test Files  1 passed (1)
        Tests  1 passed | 65 skipped (66)
```

Both workflows parse as valid YAML and pass `bash -n`.

## What was not tested

- Full end-to-end OpenGrep scan pipeline (requires valid OpenGrep API token + runner). The timeout behavior is demonstrated at the curl level with scaled deadlines.
- IPv6 stall scenarios. The workflow uses standard GitHub Actions networking, which is IPv4-only in practice.

target.title: refactor(plugin-sdk): isolate core session state from plugin mutations
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an isolation gap where core-owned restart-recovery coordination could be exposed, overwritten, or lost through Plugin SDK session APIs.

Upstream now persists channel-turn recovery fields under the `restartRecovery*` namespace. This PR keeps those shipped fields, as well as the later split series' `mainRestartRecovery` aggregate, out of plugin reads, callback inputs, replacements, ACP resolution, and injected runtime surfaces.

The repair also addresses two earlier review findings: an identity-preserving whole-store key move could silently drop private recovery state, and the ACP SDK declared that it returned the internal `AcpSessionManager` class even though the runtime object was already a restricted facade.

## Why This Change Was Made

Plugin-visible session rows now pass through one projection/reconciliation owner. The public `SessionEntry` type omits `mainRestartRecovery` and the complete `restartRecovery*` namespace, matching runtime behavior.

Private recovery state is retained for same-key updates and for a unique one-to-one `sessionId` key move. It is not copied when the source or destination mapping is ambiguous, and it is cleared when the effective session identity changes. Future `restartRecovery*` plugin extension slots are reserved before a new core field can collide with them.

The ACP getter returns an explicit `AcpSessionManagerFacade` interface. The runtime object remains stable, frozen, null-prototype, and limited to bound public methods, so plugins cannot reach the internal manager constructor or bypass session projection.

Compatibility note: released `v2026.7.1-beta.5` / `v2026.7.1` and the frozen PR #96230 returned the real manager class. This PR intentionally does not preserve `instanceof`, prototype, or constructor identity because exposing the internal constructor would reopen the private-session-state escape path. The SDK catalog documents that contract for maintainer review.

## User Impact

Plugin authors continue to use the same session and ACP methods, while current and future core restart-recovery coordination remains private and survives valid session-key moves.

Plugins that relied on `getAcpSessionManager()` being an actual internal class instance must migrate to the structural `AcpSessionManagerFacade` contract. No session schema, storage format, ACP method behavior, retry budget, or production `mainRestartRecovery` writer is added by this PR.

## Evidence

- Recovery isolation matrix: 9 files, 82/82 tests passed across direct Plugin SDK APIs, modern and deprecated whole-store mutation, unique and ambiguous key moves, ACP, agent runtime, channel runtime, combined transcript-store reads, injection rejection, and session identity rotation.
- Plugin SDK surface budget tests: 10/10 passed.
- Public API contract: generated declarations expose the projected `SessionEntry` and `AcpSessionManagerFacade`; no `mainRestartRecovery` or `restartRecovery*` declaration remains in the generated SDK baseline.
- Plugin SDK API baseline, public export budget, formatting, lint, max-lines ratchet, and diff-check passed after syncing to exact base `2848acbbaa18f120d257557b1cfb6939f383dcc6`.
- Upstream reduced the public Plugin SDK export baseline to 7,952 during the sync; this PR's reviewed `AcpSessionManagerFacade` is the sole additional export, for a passing budget of 7,953.
- Source audit found no remaining critical, major, minor, security, performance, persistence, or public-contract issue.
- Frozen PR comparison at `edc24088387a8d573798233979a71f3b40a24ac9` confirms that its whole-store implementation lacked cross-key recovery transfer and its ACP SDK returned the internal class directly.
- The branch contains zero production `mainRestartRecovery` producers. Existing upstream `restartRecovery*` writers remain unchanged and now sit behind the Plugin SDK projection boundary.

Protected local TypeScript validation could not be recorded because this machine cannot attest the required cgroup limits; the guard stopped before execution and was not bypassed. GitHub CI remains the authoritative protected typecheck/build lane.

Per maintainer-requested workflow for this split, the final audit is a complete code-diff/source review rather than a separate automated final-review pass.

target.title: fix(agents): skip sender-scoped tool policy when sender identity is absent
target.body:
## What Problem This Solves

A spawned subagent loses tools granted by an exact `toolsBySender` sender override because its internal session has no sender identity and falls through to the wildcard `"*"` policy, silently stripping filesystem and runtime tools.
- Problem: `resolveSenderToolPolicy` resolves sender-scoped tool policy even when no sender identity exists, matching the wildcard `"*"` entry and stripping tools from identity-less subagent sessions
- Solution: Skip sender-scoped resolution entirely when all sender fields (`senderId`, `senderName`, `senderUsername`, `senderE164`) are null/undefined — the subagent inherits the parent's already-resolved tool policy
- What changed: `src/agents/sender-tool-policy.ts` (early return when sender identity is absent)
- What did NOT change: spawn/session lifecycle, config schema, tool policy for sessions with sender identity

## Change Type (select all)

- [x] Bug fix
- [ ] Feature
- [ ] Refactor required for the fix
- [ ] Docs
- [ ] Security hardening
- [ ] Chore/infra

## Scope (select all)

- [ ] Gateway / orchestration
- [x] Skills / tool execution
- [ ] Auth / tokens
- [ ] Memory / storage
- [ ] Integrations
- [ ] API / contracts
- [ ] UI / DX
- [ ] CI/CD / infra

## Linked Issue/PR

- Fixes #109025
- [x] This PR fixes a bug or regression

## Motivation

When a WhatsApp sender configured with an E164 `toolsBySender` override spawns a subagent via `sessions_spawn`, the subagent resolves its own tool policy. Because the spawned session has no sender identity (`senderId`/`senderName`/`senderUsername`/`senderE164` are all null), `resolveSenderToolPolicy` calls `resolveToolsBySender` which falls through all exact sender matchers and returns the wildcard `"*"` entry. This strips 31 tools (including filesystem and runtime tools) from the subagent, leaving only ~6 generic tools.

The parent already resolved the correct sender-scoped policy — the subagent should inherit that result, not re-resolve from scratch without a sender identity.

## Evidence

- Behavior addressed: spawned subagent re-resolves `toolsBySender` without sender identity, matching wildcard `"*"` and losing filesystem/runtime tools
- Real environment tested: Linux, Node 22.19, `fix/subagent-sender-tool-policy-109025`
- Exact steps or command run after this patch:

```bash
# Unit tests pass (existing behavior preserved)
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/config/group-policy.test.ts --run
node scripts/run-vitest.mjs src/agents/agent-tools.policy.test.ts --run

# Format check
npx oxfmt --check src/agents/sender-tool-policy.ts

# Lint check
```

`resolveSenderToolPolicy` → `resolveToolsBySender` → `matchToolsBySenderPolicy` falls through all exact sender matchers and returns `compiled.wildcard` when no sender field matches. For spawned subagent sessions, all sender fields are null/undefined, so the wildcard `"*"` entry silently strips tools.

- **Provenance**: `introduced by` the sender tool policy system (the wildcard fallback is inherent to the `toolsBySender` design, not a recent regression)

- **Best fix**: Yes. target.title: fix(security): narrow sandbox parent to exact active session workspace to prevent cross-agent media read (#107972)
target.body:
Closes #107972

## What Problem This Solves

Fixes an issue where an agent's sandbox-generated media (images, PDFs, previews, attachments) could be read by a sibling agent in a different session. When both agents have sandbox directories under the shared `<stateDir>/sandboxes/` parent, the baseline media root allowlist includes the entire parent directory. Agent-scoped media roots forward this broad parent without narrowing it to the exact active sandbox workspace, so any path under a sibling sandbox directory passes containment checks.

## Why This Change Was Made

The root cause is in `getAgentScopedMediaLocalRoots`: it starts from `buildMediaLocalRoots`, which includes `<stateDir>/sandboxes` as a single entry, and only appends the agent workspace directory. It never replaces the broad sandboxes parent with the precise active sandbox workspace path. Meanwhile, the `workspace-*` sibling exclusion in `assertLocalMediaAllowed` only fires when `localRoots === undefined`, but agent-facing callers always pass explicit roots, so that defense is bypassed.

The fix adds an optional `sandboxWorkspaceDir` parameter to `getAgentScopedMediaLocalRoots`. When provided, the function removes the broad `sandboxes/` parent from the roots list and adds the caller-supplied exact sandbox workspace path instead. The replacement is unconditional: it runs before agent-id early returns, so supplying an exact sandbox path narrows access even when agentId is absent or the agent workspace cannot be resolved.

The parameter is threaded through `getAgentScopedMediaLocalRootsForSources` and `resolveAgentScopedOutboundMediaAccess`. Only callers with existing sandbox context (`message-action-runner`, where `input.sandboxRoot` is already available) pass this parameter; other callers (`control-ui`, `send`) omit it, preserving backward compatibility. No new configuration options, environment variables, or file paths are introduced.

## User Impact

Cross-session sibling sandbox media access is prevented. A sandbox workspace can no longer reference files from another sandbox workspace under the shared `sandboxes/` parent. All legitimate sandbox media flows (outbound attachments, Control UI previews, media-understanding results) continue to work — the fix narrows authorization without changing the set of accessible paths for the owning session.

## Evidence

**Real-behavior proof** — standalone harness that imports production `getAgentScopedMediaLocalRoots`, `getAgentScopedMediaLocalRootsForSources`, `getDefaultMediaLocalRoots`, and `assertLocalMediaAllowed` from `.ts` source via `tsx`, creates real sibling sandbox directories on a temp filesystem, and exercises the full authorization path with zero mocks:

```
Production source: file://///media/vdb/outcoco/checklang/bak3/src/media/local-roots.ts

=== S1: sandboxWorkspaceDir + valid agent (happy path) ===
  roots: sandboxes/ present=false — PASS
  roots: sandboxWs present=true — PASS
  SIBLING: REJECTED (path-not-allowed) — PASS
  OWN: ALLOWED — PASS

=== S2: no sandboxWorkspaceDir (backward compat) ===
  roots: sandboxes/ present=true (expected true) — PASS

=== S3: agentId = undefined + sandboxWorkspaceDir ===
  roots: sandboxes/ present=false — PASS
  roots: sandboxWs present=true — PASS
  SIBLING: REJECTED (path-not-allowed) — PASS

=== S4: unresolved workspace + sandboxWorkspaceDir ===
  roots: sandboxes/ present=false — PASS
  roots: sandboxWs present=true — PASS
  SIBLING: REJECTED (path-not-allowed) — PASS

=== S5: getAgentScopedMediaLocalRootsForSources + sandboxWorkspaceDir ===
  roots: sandboxes/ present=false (expected false) — PASS
  roots: sandboxWs present=true (expected true) — PASS

=== S6: getDefaultMediaLocalRoots (non-agent) ===
  sandboxes/ in roots: true — PASS

=== RESULTS: 7 passed, 0 failed ===
```

**Unit tests** — 13/13 passing in `local-roots.test.ts` (4 new, 9 existing), 8/8 passing in `read-capability.test.ts`, 21/21 total across media tests:

- "replaces sandboxes parent with exact sandbox workspace when sandboxWorkspaceDir provided"
- "keeps sandboxes parent when sandboxWorkspaceDir is not provided (backward compat)"
- "replaces sandboxes parent with sandboxWorkspaceDir when agentId is absent"
- "replaces sandboxes parent with sandboxWorkspaceDir when agent workspace is unresolved"

**Lint** — 0 warnings, 0 errors (oxlint on all changed files).

**Lines changed** — 4 files modified (`local-roots.ts`, `local-roots.test.ts`, `read-capability.ts`, `message-action-runner.ts`). Non-test: +37 insertions.

**Codex review** — [All findings addressed](https://github.com/openclaw/openclaw/pull/107972#issuecomment-XXXXX). The initial implementation placed the sandbox replacement after agent-id early returns, creating a fail-open branch when agentId was absent or workspace unresolved. Codex review identified this ([P1] Apply sandbox narrowing before agent-workspace early returns). The fix was moved ahead of early returns, and real-behavior proof was added for all three agent identity states (resolved, absent, unresolved).

---

This PR is AI-assisted. Analysis, implementation, and testing were performed using AI tools (opencode) with review and validation by the author.
